A1:
**A1 — Calls isAvailable with a String argument.**

Award the point if the response contains at least one syntactically correct invocation of the availability method with an argument that is evidently the candidate username string, made either on the class `Account`, on `this`, on an unqualified bare call inside the `Account` class (e.g., `isAvailable(requestedName)`, since "use of `this` is optional" covers the implicit class/`this` receiver), or on any reference whose type is `Account` (e.g., `acct.isAvailable(s)` or `new Account(...).isAvailable(s)`) — an `Account` reference is still "on Account," the call compiles, and the restriction is meant only to exclude calls made on unrelated classes or objects such as a `String`, a `Scanner`, or a student-invented class. Treat the argument generously: the point stands for a `String` other than the parameter, an undeclared name variable, a value the student plainly treats as text, or a call written with the type word included; only an argument clearly not intended as a string — such as a loop counter used as a number — fails this part. Minor spelling or capitalization variants of the method name (`isAvailible`, `IsAvailable`, `is_available`) do not cost the point so long as context makes the intended call to the availability method unambiguous, since the point is for making the call. If the response makes one correct call and also contains a stray, leftover, or malformed invocation elsewhere, still award the point.

Deduct only when no correct call exists anywhere in the response — that is, when every invocation either uses an explicit receiver that is not `Account` or `this` (e.g., a `String`, `Scanner`, or unrelated object), passes an argument clearly not meant as the username string, or is otherwise malformed such that no single syntactically correct call on `Account`/`this` with a string argument remains.
A3:
**A3 — Increments a count (in the context of a loop)**

Award the point (no_deduct) whenever the response contains a counter whose value actually advances once per repetition attempt. The advance must be a real update that executes on each attempt — a statement such as `count++`, `i++`, `suffix++`, or `count = count + 1` inside the body of the repetition, or, for a recursive solution, passing `count + 1` (or an equivalent) on each recursive call. The repetition mechanism itself does not matter: a `while`/`for`/`do-while` loop and a recursive helper that re-attempts with an advanced counter both satisfy "in the context of a loop," since the intent of the item is that the counter advances per attempt, not that any particular loop syntax appears. Declaration and initialization of the counter are irrelevant here: give the point even if the variable is never initialized, and even if it is never declared anywhere at all (so the code would not compile), as long as the incrementing statement appears inside the loop or repeated-attempt structure. Likewise, failing to use the count as part of a possible username does not cost the point.

Deduct only when the counter's value never actually changes per repetition — for example, a counter that is merely declared (or declared and initialized) and then only read inside the loop, with no `++`, `+ 1`, or equivalent update executing on each attempt. A single increment that cannot occur per attempt in any repeated structure likewise fails.
